title: The Power of Belonging: How Family Bonds and Community Protect Against Suicide st-suicide
author: Jason Manning
summary: Sociologist Jason Manning argues that suicide risk falls as social integration rises, and that marriage and parenthood are among the most consequential forms of integration. Building on Durkheim, he surveys roughly 130 years of evidence, including a study of 34,000 men over 24 years, a Norwegian register study and a 2025 US study finding married people about three times less likely to consider, plan or attempt suicide. He notes the gap between married and unmarried people appears to be growing and is no longer mostly a male phenomenon. Because people do not marry at random, he considers whether the link is causal, and offers five plausible mechanisms: meaning, belonging, social support, structured responsibilities and social monitoring. The piece is a research synthesis rather than a causal proof, and it opens with a note directing readers to the 988 crisis line.
points: Suicide risk declines as people become more enmeshed in ties to individuals and institutions, a pattern traced from Durkheim to modern studies.
Evidence from the US, Norway, Sweden, South Korea and Hong Kong finds married people and parents at lower risk than the unmarried and childless.
A 2025 US study found the married-unmarried gap in suicide attempts has grown, and a 2024 analysis found only a small gender gap in marriage's protective effect.
Manning proposes five mechanisms: meaning and purpose, belongingness, social support, the structuring effect of family responsibilities, and social monitoring and control.
He acknowledges selection effects, since people do not marry at random, but argues the plausible mechanisms make a causal reading credible.
quotes: What it means is that, all else equal, someone’s risk of committing suicide declines to the extent they are enmeshed in social ties to individuals and institutions. Bonds of family, friendship, and community exert a protective effect against self-destruction.
And one study tracking 34,000 U.S. men for 24 years showed that scoring high on a 7-item index of social integration was associated with a two-fold reduction in suicide risk.
Likewise, nearly 130 years of research shows that the bonds of marriage and parenthood are especially consequential when it comes to suicide.
For example, an analysis of over one million U.S. adults found that never-married persons were 48% more likely to commit suicide than those who were either married or living with a partner.
In the U.S., a 2025 study by Stephen Cranney and Samuel Wilkinson found that being married predicted a lower risk of nonfatal suicide behavior for both men and women.
Durkheim recognized this long ago, arguing that people need something greater than themselves to justify the trials of life.

Routines of work and child care give structure to daily life, and a reason to keep going. Responsibilities mitigate against excessive drinking, gambling, and other risky behaviors that can themselves be risk factors for suicide.

Close social bonds transform suicide, drug abuse, and various other risky behaviors from matters of personal preference to matters of right and wrong, and from a prerogative of the individual to something with clear consequences for others.
